subsections.title: U.S.-China relations / Trump-Xi follow-ups
subsections.text: Preparations are advancing for the third Trump-Xi summit of 2026 on the sidelines of the APEC leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen (18–19 November), with a further encounter expected at the G20 in Florida in December. Agenda items include trade commitments under the Boards of Trade and Investment, agricultural and rare-earth purchases, and super-intelligence (SI) risk management (pre-release model evaluation, human control, and an incident-reporting channel). Secretary of State Rubio and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi have coordinated logistics; Treasury Secretary Bessent is accompanying Trump. A possible U.S.-China-Russia trilateral on the APEC sidelines has been confirmed by the White House, focusing on Iran and nuclear issues rather than Ukraine. Post-midterm Republican losses have slightly improved Beijing’s near-term negotiating leverage, though longer-term congressional pressure on Taiwan arms sales and export controls remains. A low-level military crisis-management framework is under discussion, though analysts note it is inadequate for nuclear or major flashpoint crises.

subsections.title: U.S.-Iran conflict & Middle East (including Houthis)
subsections.text: Iran and its allies intensified pressure over the weekend. The IRGC claimed drone attacks on U.S. radar sites at Riffa Air Base in Bahrain (disputed by CENTCOM, which reported intercepts with no damage). Iranian naval forces alleged mines struck tankers near the Strait of Hormuz. In Yemen, Saudi-backed government-aligned forces withdrew from Red Sea coastal positions near Bab al-Mandeb and Dhubab, allowing Houthi advances that threaten the approaches to Aden; Houthis also launched ballistic missiles toward Saudi targets. President Trump has indicated to advisers he may hold off on further strikes absent fresh provocations, favoring economic pressure. Shipping through Hormuz remains disrupted relative to pre-conflict norms.

subsections.title: Ukraine-Russia
subsections.text: Day ~1726–1727 of the full-scale invasion saw continued high-intensity fighting (171 combat engagements reported on 14 November) and reciprocal long-range strikes on energy, industrial, and civilian infrastructure. Russian personnel losses were estimated by Ukrainian sources at ~2,230 in the prior 24 hours (cumulative ~1.62 million). U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi produced no breakthrough; U.S. negotiators reportedly floated Ukrainian NATO membership in exchange for full withdrawal from Donbas—an idea rejected by Moscow’s maximalist demands. Ukraine continues deep strikes on Russian oil facilities. Front lines have seen limited net Russian gains in recent months amid high attrition. Other developments include Estonia’s decision to close border crossings with Russia following a reported sabotage attempt and ongoing Black Sea shipping risks.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: China formally extended the suspension of its additional 24% tariff on U.S. goods for two months (through 10 January 2027), retaining a 10% blanket tariff. Parallel extensions cover special port fees on U.S.-linked vessels, certain export-control and entity-list measures, and rare-earth-related waivers. The United States likewise extended relevant Section 301 exclusions and related pauses. These steps implement the September Washington summit consensus that prolonged the Busan-era truce. Reciprocal tariff reductions on roughly $30 billion of non-sensitive goods per side remain under discussion via the Board of Trade, alongside agricultural purchase commitments. No major new tariff actions were announced in recent days; both sides continue to press for fuller implementation of existing pledges ahead of the Shenzhen summit. China has flagged that it will monitor any U.S. shift toward Section 301 tariffs as a replacement for previously invalidated IEEPA measures.

sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text: Hyperscaler capital expenditure guidance for 2026 is exceptionally large (combined Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, and Microsoft figures in the $700+ billion range), crowding out capacity elsewhere in the electronics supply chain. Semiconductor capex growth forecasts have been revised upward (one tracker now near +34% for 2026). Acute concentration risks persist in leading-edge logic and packaging (TSMC CoWoS and HBM), rare-earth magnets and processing (China dominant), power equipment (transformers, turbines, grid interconnection lead times of years), and specialty materials (gallium, germanium). PCB, laminate, and memory tightness is already visible in longer lead times and higher prices. Power availability and political pushback against new data-center construction in some U.S. jurisdictions add further constraints. Diversification efforts are under way but will take years to materially reduce bottlenecks.

subsections.text: The conflict continues with intermittent shipping disruptions in and around the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian forces have claimed additional mine strikes on commercial vessels (including tankers and a liquefied gas carrier in mid-November), though U.S. assessments indicate routes have been cleared and no confirmed re-mining. The U.S. maintains a naval blockade and economic pressure (CENTCOM Task Force elements), while signaling restraint on further strikes absent new provocations. Houthis have launched ballistic missiles and drones against Yemeni government-aligned forces in Lahij and against Saudi targets (including pipeline pumping stations, oil facilities, and Riyadh-area infrastructure). Saudi-led forces have conducted airstrikes in response. Trump has indicated willingness to hold off on escalatory action unless provoked, amid ongoing indirect talks and Iranian demands (end of blockade, asset release, sanctions relief, etc.). Shipping volumes through Hormuz remain well below pre-war levels despite partial recovery in Gulf exports.

subsections.title: Ukraine-Russia
subsections.text: Trilateral talks (Ukraine, Russia, U.S.) took place in Abu Dhabi this week, with discussion of expanding future rounds to include European representatives and working toward a large-scale prisoner exchange (potentially up to 1,500 per side). Positions remain firm: Russia insists on Ukrainian neutrality, demilitarization, and territorial elements; Ukraine and the West emphasize security guarantees. Battlefield activity continues with Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, hospitals (including Kyiv), and cities (Zaporizhzhia, Odesa), plus Ukrainian drone/missile attacks on Russian industrial and energy targets (e.g., Volgograd region). Starshield satellite system speed restrictions have limited Ukrainian interception capabilities. A Russian warship was reportedly struck in the Gulf of Finland. Overall trajectory points toward a possible negotiated endgame, though core gaps on territory and security architecture persist. Day count is approximately 1,725.

Houthis (Iran-backed) have escalated attacks on Saudi critical infrastructure, including claimed strikes on Riyadh’s financial district (damaging an Aramco building), airports, and other sites; Saudi air defenses have intercepted multiple missiles and drones. Ground fighting continues in Yemen. Oil market participants cite an elevated risk of resumed broader fighting. Ukraine-Russia: Intense Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure have caused widespread blackouts (hundreds of thousands without power in eastern regions; external power briefly lost at Zaporizhzhia). Russia reported strikes on cargo vessels in the Black Sea and substations. U.S.-brokered trilateral talks (Ukraine, Russia, U.S.) are scheduled in Abu Dhabi for 10–11 November. Battlefield advances remain incremental; Ukrainian strikes continue on Russian oil/refining and logistics targets. Day ~1,719 of the full-scale invasion.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: The U.S.-China trade truce (originating in the October 2025 Busan agreement and extended in September 2026) runs to 10 January 2027. USTR has proposed (and, per some reports, formalized elements of) extension of maritime action suspensions and product exclusions through early January. Overall U.S. tariff rates on Chinese goods remain elevated (around the 20%+ range under various authorities post-IEEPA voiding). China has committed to rare-earth and critical-mineral flows, agricultural purchases (including coal), and limited export-control relaxations, though fulfillment is incomplete. Reciprocal tariff cuts on ~$30 billion of non-sensitive goods per side are under discussion via the Board of Trade. Prediction markets price a high probability that elevated tariffs persist into early 2027. Other bilateral frictions (UFLPA entity list additions, overcapacity probes) continue.

sections.title: Macro Currency Interventions

subsections.text: The Japanese yen remains under pressure near USD/JPY 158.3–158.5. The Bank of Japan holds its policy rate at 1.25% (raised earlier in 2026) with a split vote and further hikes under discussion (December odds elevated but not certain). The Ministry of Finance has conducted large-scale yen-buying interventions in 2026 (records include ~¥11.7 trillion in April–May and a record ~¥15.4 trillion in the July–August period, including the first coordinated U.S.-Japan operation since 1998). Officials have repeatedly signaled readiness to act against disorderly moves near the 160 level; no new intervention is reported in the most recent published period (late September–October). The wide U.S.-Japan rate differential and current-account dynamics continue to weigh on the yen. Broader central-bank trends: Fed funds effective rate ~3.88% (target range 3.75–4.00%); markets price a high probability of a further 25 bp hike in December. ECB and others remain on hold or data-dependent amid sticky services inflation.

sections.title: Energy Markets & Oil Prices

subsections.text: Brent settled near $98.3 and WTI near $90.8 on 6 November (Friday), down roughly 13% on the week, with weekend quotes holding in the $97–98 / $90 range. The sharp weekly decline reflected positioning around potential U.S.-Iran de-escalation, though no deal has been announced and tanker incidents plus Houthi activity continue. Key drivers: Strait of Hormuz risks, Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure, OPEC+ supply discipline, and Chinese demand. Risks are skewed to the upside on any resumption of broader kinetic action (some analysts assign high odds). Short-term outlook: prices remain elevated relative to pre-conflict levels; next catalysts include U.S. data, EIA outlook, and OPEC monthly report. Natural gas is comparatively subdued (~$3 Henry Hub).

sections.title: Inflation, Monetary Policy & Bond Markets

subsections.text: U.S. headline CPI has been in the mid-3% range (recent readings ~3.4–3.7% YoY); core measures lower (~2.5–2.6%). October non-farm payrolls surprised to the upside (+165k, unemployment 4.1%). PCE has printed in line with expectations. The Fed held in late October; markets price ~70%+ odds of a December hike, with additional tightening priced into 2027. 10-year Treasury yield has traded ~4.84–4.95% recently (below earlier peaks above 5.3%); 2-year ~4.5%. Real yields and term premium reflect growth, debt, and AI-capex demand more than a sharp rise in inflation expectations (breakevens contained). ECB remains restrictive; BOJ is the clear outlier with gradual normalization.

sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text: Hyperscaler 2026 capex guidance is extraordinary (~$700–725 billion combined for Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft alone, up sharply from 2025). This is crowding out traditional electronics capacity, lifting PCB/laminate prices (reports of up to 40% increases), extending lead times, and prompting prepayments. Bottlenecks have shifted beyond GPUs to advanced packaging, substrates/interposers, testing, optics, power infrastructure, and specialty materials. Semiconductor capex growth forecasts have been revised higher (some to ~34% for 2026). Concentration risks remain acute in advanced chips, rare earths/critical minerals, packaging capacity, and power/grid access (local opposition has delayed or canceled numerous projects). Capital availability is also emerging as a constraint (funding-round downsizes, rating-outlook pressure). Export controls and geopolitics continue to shape equipment and materials flows.

sections.title: Interconnections & Monitoring Priorities

subsections.text: Geopolitical flashpoints (Hormuz/Houthi activity, Ukraine energy strikes) directly support elevated energy prices and inflation risks, which feed into Fed/BOJ policy divergence and yen pressure. The U.S.-China truce and AI dialogue provide a temporary buffer for supply chains and capex, yet rare-earth and packaging concentration plus power constraints create single-point failure risks that could amplify any escalation. Post-midterm U.S. politics may increase short-term Chinese leverage in trade talks while raising longer-term uncertainty. Daily/weekly watchlist: - APEC Shenzhen (17–19 Nov) and any Trump-Xi (or trilateral) outcomes on trade, rare earths, AI. - Abu Dhabi Ukraine talks (10–11 Nov) and Russian energy-strike tempo. - Iran/Hormuz/Houthi activity and oil reaction. - U.S. inflation/payrolls follow-through and December Fed pricing. - USD/JPY approach to 160 and any fresh intervention signals. - AI supply-chain lead times, packaging/power project delays, and hyperscaler funding commentary.
